title: Compulsory English: Model Question Sets and Predicted Questions
html:
The SEE English paper is one of the most regular papers a student sits: the same four reading passages, four writing tasks and ten grammar items appear in the same order every year.

This chapter sets out the grid, gives two complete model papers with answers, and ends with a ranked list of predicted questions. The ranking rests on one fact only: the grid fixes the question types and the syllabus fixes the texts.

Nothing here is a forecast of what will appear, and no question is copied from a past paper.

The grid (75 marks, 3 hours)
Part Marks Task
Reading 1 5 seen text (about 100 words), one question type
Reading 2 10 seen text (about 200 words), two question types
Reading 3 10 unseen text (about 200 words), two types
Reading 4 15 unseen text (about 300 words), three types incl. vocabulary
Guided writing I 5 paragraph, chart, instructions, notice, advertisement
Guided writing II 5 news story, skeleton story, message, biography
Free writing I 6 paragraph, application, dialogue
Free writing II 9 letter, email, essay
Grammar 10 5 reproduction items and 5 multiple-choice items in a passage

The figures follow the specification grid for Grade 10 English.

10.1 Pattern analysis

Skill Marks Share of 75 Where marks are lost
Reading (R1 to R4) 40 53% copying half a sentence; skipping the vocabulary item
Writing (four tasks) 25 33% wrong layout, no paragraphs, off the topic
Grammar 10 13% tag questions, backshift in reported speech, passive forms of perfect tenses

Timing for three hours

Reading 1 and 2: 25 minutes. Reading 3 and 4: 40 minutes. Grammar: 15 minutes (do it early; it is ten sure marks). Writing: 80 minutes (15 + 15 + 20 + 30). Check: 20 minutes.

10.2 Model Set 1

Time: 3 hours. Full marks: 75. Attempt all questions. In a real paper the seen texts are printed in the paper; here the textbook texts are named.

Question paper

Reading 1. Seen text: "Climbing" (Amy Lowell), Unit 8. Write true or false. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. The child in the poem climbs a hill. 2. The branches are compared to a staircase. 3. The poet imagines a town at the top. 4. The poem is written in free verse with no rhyme. 5. The poem is about the power of determination.

Reading 2. Seen text: "Pratap Malla", Unit 9. [10]

A. Choose the best answer. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. Pratap Malla ruledaLalitpurbBhaktapurcKantipurdPatan
  2. He took the titleaKabindrabNarendracShahendradMahendra
  3. His wealth came mainly fromafarmingbTibet–India tradectourismdgold mines
  4. He kept his state safe byawarbdiplomacycbuilding wallsdhiding
  5. Which place is linked with him?aRani PokharibRanipauwacRanighatdRani Mahal

B. Answer the questions. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. When did he rule? 7. Name one language he wrote in. 8. How did he show his interest in religion and art? 9. Which palace is linked with him? 10. What does the text show about him as a ruler?

Reading 3. Unseen text (advertisement). [10]

HIMALAYAN COMPUTER TRAINING CENTRE, Butwal Three-month Basic Computer Course starts on 1 Baisakh. Classes run from 6 a.m. to 8 a.m. every day except Saturday.

Course fee: Rs 6,000 (Rs 5,000 for SEE graduates who register before 20 Chaitra). Only 20 seats. Certificate and free practice hours. Call 071-555123 or visit our office near the bus park.

A. True or false. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. The course lasts three months. 2. Classes are held on Saturdays. 3. SEE graduates can get a discount. 4. The centre has unlimited seats. 5. The office is near the airport.

B. Answer briefly. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. When do the classes start? 7. How much is the fee for a SEE graduate who registers early? 8. How many seats are there? 9. What will the students receive at the end? 10. How can a person contact the centre?

Reading 4. Unseen text. [15]

Nepal is rich in water, yet many towns face water shortage every spring. Rivers fall from the Himalayas, but towns lie far from rivers, and old pipes leak much of the water before it reaches homes.

In some cities people queue at taps or buy water from tankers, which costs more than piped water.

Experts say that saving water begins at home. A tap that drips all night can waste many litres, and a washing machine used for half a load wastes both water and electricity.

Schools can help by teaching children to turn off taps and to collect rainwater. Some communities in the hills have built small ponds to catch rain, and their springs have started to flow again after years.

The government has also begun to repair old pipes and to build long water-supply schemes. But the shortage will end only when every citizen sees water as a shared and limited resource, not as a free gift that never ends.

A. Choose the best answer. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. Towns face a water shortage becausearivers have dried upbtowns are far from rivers and pipes leakcthere is no raindpeople drink too much
  2. Water bought from tankers isacheaper than piped waterbcostlier than piped watercfreedcleaner than spring water
  3. Which action is advised for schools?acut pipesbturn off taps and collect rainwatercbuy tankersdbuild roads
  4. Hill communities builtaponds to catch rainbdamscwellsdcanals
  5. The writer's main point is thatawater is unlimitedbcitizens must see water as a limited shared resourceconly the government can helpdtankers are best

B. Answer the questions. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. What happens to water in old pipes? 7. Name one way to save water at home. 8. What did the ponds do for the springs? 9. What is the government doing? 10. Why is water not a "free gift that never ends"?

C. Vocabulary. Find words in the passage that mean: [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. a situation in which there is not enough of something 12. to gather and keep (rainwater) 13. a plan to supply something, as for water 14. to let a liquid escape through a hole 15. something useful, such as water, that people use

Guided writing I. [5] The table shows the number of books borrowed from a school library in three months: Shrawan 210, Bhadra 150, Ashwin 90. Write a paragraph of about 100 words describing it.

Guided writing II. [5] Write a news story from these clues: Fire — Dharan bazaar — 8 shops — midnight — firefighters — no one hurt.

Free writing I. [6] Write an application to the head teacher asking to be excused from school fees because your father has lost his job. (about 150 words)

Free writing II. [9] Write an essay of about 200 words on The Importance of Reading Books.

Grammar. [10]

A. Reproduction. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. (Tense) She ____ (teach) English for ten years now.
  2. (Question tag) Nobody called, ____?
  3. (Reported speech) "I am going to Pokhara," said Nisha.
  4. (Voice) The students are cleaning the classroom.
  5. (Negation) Everyone enjoyed the film. (Make it negative with No one.)

B. Choose the correct word. [5 x 1 = 5] Last winter I went (6) ____ a village (7) ____ the hills. The village (8) ____ I stayed was small.

(9) ____ it was cold, the people were warm. If I (10) ____ more time, I would stay longer.

  1. ainbtocatdby
  2. aofbincatdon
  3. awhobwherecwhosedwhom
  4. aAlthoughbDespitecBecausedSo
  5. ahavebhad hadchaddwould have

Answers to Model Set 1

Reading 1 and 2

R1. 1. False — an apple tree. 2. True. 3. True. 4. False — the poem has rhyming couplets. 5. True. R2 A. 1. (c) 2. (a) 3. (b) 4. (b) 5. (a). R2 B. 6. About 1641–1674. 7.

Any one language of the many he wrote in (the text says he wrote in many languages). 8. He built and repaired temples and palaces, which showed his devotion and his love of art. 9. Hanuman Dhoka. 10.

That he was a wise, cultured ruler who used diplomacy, trade and the arts.

Reading 3

A. 1. True. 2. False — every day except Saturday. 3. True. 4. False — only 20 seats. 5. False — near the bus park. B. 6. On 1 Baisakh. 7. Rs 5,000. 8. Twenty. 9. A certificate. 10. By calling 071-555123 or visiting the office near the bus park.

Reading 4

A. 1. (b) 2. (b) 3. (b) 4. (a) 5. (b). B. 6. Much of it leaks out before it reaches homes. 7. Turn off dripping taps (or use a full load in the washing machine). 8. They made the springs flow again after years. 9.

It is repairing old pipes and building long water-supply schemes. 10. Because the supply is limited and shared; careless use will end the shortage only if people change. C. 11. shortage. 12. collect. 13. scheme. 14. leak. 15. resource.

Guided writing I: model

The table shows how many books pupils borrowed from the school library in three months. Borrowing was highest in Shrawan, when 210 books were taken. In Bhadra it fell to 150, and it fell again to 90 in Ashwin, the lowest figure.

So the number in Ashwin was less than half of that in Shrawan. The decline may be due to examinations or festival holidays. The library should therefore hold reading events in Ashwin to encourage students to borrow more books.

Guided writing II: model

Fire destroys eight shops in Dharan

Dharan, 18 Magh. Eight shops were burnt down in a fire that broke out in Dharan bazaar at midnight. Firefighters arrived within twenty minutes and brought the blaze under control by dawn. No one was hurt, because the shops were closed.

The cause of the fire is not yet known and police are investigating. Traders have asked the municipality for help.

Free writing I: model

15 Magh 2082

The Head Teacher Shree Mahendra Secondary School Biratnagar

Subject: Request for a fee waiver

Sir,

I am a student of Grade 10. My father lost his job two months ago and our family is finding it hard to pay my fees. I have always been regular and have passed every examination with good marks.

I request you to excuse me from the school fees for this year. I will study hard and keep the honour of the school. I am attaching a letter from my ward office.

Yours obediently, Roshan Karki Grade 10, Roll No. 7

Free writing II: model

The Importance of Reading Books

Books are the oldest and best friends of mankind. In this age of phones and videos, reading is still one of the most useful habits a student can have.

First, reading improves language. A person who reads widely learns new words and how sentences are built, and writes better. Second, books give knowledge: a single book can carry the experience of a lifetime.

Third, reading relaxes the mind; a good story takes us away from worry. It also trains concentration, which students need for study.

Yet many young people read nothing but their textbooks. Libraries are empty while screens are busy. Schools should therefore hold reading hours and give prizes to readers. Parents should buy books as gifts.

In conclusion, a person who reads is never alone and never ignorant. We should read at least a little every day.

Grammar

A. 1. has been teaching (or has taught) — for ten years shows a period up to now. 2. did they — nobody makes the clause negative, so the tag is positive. 3. Nisha said that she was going to Pokhara. 4.

The classroom is being cleaned by the students. 5. No one enjoyed the film. B. 6. (b) to. 7. (b) in. 8. (b) where. 9. (a) Although. 10. (c) had — second conditional: if + past, would + base verb.

10.3 Model Set 2

Time: 3 hours. Full marks: 75.

Question paper

Reading 1. Seen text: "Weathers" (Thomas Hardy), Unit 14. Fill in the gaps. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. The poem was written by ____. 2. The refrain of each stanza is "And so do ____." 3. The speaker likes ____ weather. 4. The weather he shuns is ____ weather. 5. Each stanza has ____ lines.

Reading 2. Seen text: "Strange Food from Around the World", Unit 6. [10]

A. Match the food with its country. [5 x 1 = 5]

Food Country
1. haggis (a) France
2. shiokara (b) Scotland
3. bún riêu (c) Japan
4. snails (d) Vietnam
5. jellyfish (e) China

B. Answer the questions. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. What does the idiom a bridge too far mean? 7. Why is some food "strange"? 8. Name one food eaten as bush food in Australia. 9. Name one Vietnamese food mentioned in the text. 10. What is the writer's attitude to strange foods?

Reading 3. Unseen text (diary entry). [10]

Tuesday, 14 Kartik. Today was the most tiring day of my life, but also the happiest. We left Pokhara at five in the morning for the Sarangkot sunrise. The road was dark and my sister felt sick in the bus, so we stopped twice.

At the top, nobody spoke when the first light touched Machhapuchhre; the whole range turned gold. On the way down, we lost the path and walked for an hour before we found a tea shop.

The owner gave us hot lemon tea and would not take any money. I am writing this with sore legs, but I know I will remember this day forever.

A. Choose the best answer. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. They left Pokhara ata4 a.m.b5 a.m.c6 a.m.d7 a.m.
  2. The bus stopped twice becauseait broke downbthe writer's sister felt sickcof raindof a landslide
  3. The mountain turned gold whenathe first light touched itbthe moon rosecit snoweddit rained
  4. They foundaa hotelba tea shopca templeda police post
  5. The writer feltatired but happybangrycboreddafraid

B. Answer briefly. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. Why did they go to Sarangkot? 7. What did the group do when the light came? 8. How did they get lost? 9. What did the tea-shop owner do? 10. Why does the writer say the day was both tiring and happy?

Reading 4. Unseen text. [15]

Online learning has grown quickly in Nepal in the last few years. During the lockdowns of 2020, schools that had never used a computer began to teach through mobile phones, radio and television.

Some children in remote villages learned from radio lessons because there was no internet at all.

Teachers report that online classes have clear benefits. Students can watch a lesson again and again, and a good teacher in the capital can reach a classroom in Humla. Study material is cheaper and easier to share.

But there are problems as well. Many homes do not have a smartphone, and where they do, the signal is weak. Younger children lose attention in front of a screen, and a student cannot ask questions as easily as in a classroom.

Most educators now believe that the best way is a mixture: ordinary classes supported by online material. That way each method fills the gaps of the other.

A. Choose the best answer. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. During the lockdowns some children learned fromanewspapers onlybradio lessonsclettersdnothing
  2. A benefit of online classes is thatastudents can replay lessonsbthe signal is strongcthere are no teachersdthey cost more
  3. A problem mentioned is thataevery home has a computerbyounger children lose attentioncteachers are lazydlessons are too short
  4. Most educators preferaonly online classesbonly classroom classesca mixture of bothdno classes
  5. The passage is mainly aboutathe benefits and problems of online learningbradioclockdownsdteachers in Humla

B. Answer the questions. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. What did schools use to teach during the lockdowns? 7. How can a village class benefit from a teacher in the capital? 8. Why is it hard for students to ask questions online? 9. Why do many homes find it hard to use online lessons? 10. What do educators now believe is the best way?

C. Vocabulary: match the words (1 mark each) [5]

  1. remote 12. benefit 13. signal 14. mixture 15. educatoraa combinationbfar from townscan advantageda teacherea sign sent by wave

Guided writing I. [5] Write instructions for making a paper boat.

Guided writing II. [5] Complete the story: A shepherd boy — cried "wolf" for fun — villagers came — no wolf — a real wolf came — no one believed him. Give a moral.

Free writing I. [6] Write a dialogue between a shopkeeper and a customer who wants to return a faulty phone. (about 150 words)

Free writing II. [9] Write a letter to your friend telling him or her about a trip you took with your class. (about 200 words)

Grammar. [10]

A. Reproduction. [5 x 1 = 5]

  1. (Tense) By next April I ____ (finish) my SEE.
  2. (Question tag) I am late, ____?
  3. (Reported speech) "Where do you live?" the officer asked me.
  4. (Voice) Someone has stolen my bicycle.
  5. (Interrogation) She goes to school by bus. (Make it a question beginning How.)

B. Choose the correct word. [5 x 1 = 5] The number of visitors (6) ____ increasing. A number of them (7) ____ in homestays. They (8) ____ the guide to take them to the village.

(9) ____ it was raining, they went out. If it (10) ____ tomorrow, they will stay.

  1. aarebiscweredhave
  2. astaysbstaycis stayingdhas stayed
  3. ahadbgotcletdmade
  4. aDespitebAlthoughcBecausedSo
  5. arainsbwill raincraineddwould rain

Answers to Model Set 2

Reading 1 and 2

R1. 1. Thomas Hardy. 2. I. 3. spring. 4. winter. 5. nine. R2 A. 1. (b) 2. (c) 3. (d) 4. (a) 5. (e). R2 B. 6. Too extreme. 7.

It is strange because it is unfamiliar to people of another culture, although it is normal for the people who eat it. 8. Any bush food named in the text. 9. bún riêu. 10.

The writer treats strange foods as an adventure and says taste is cultural.

Reading 3

A. 1. (b) 2. (b) 3. (a) 4. (b) 5. (a). B. 6. To see the sunrise (over Machhapuchhre). 7. Nobody spoke; they watched the whole range turn gold. 8. They lost the path on the way down and walked for an hour. 9.

He gave them hot lemon tea and would not take any money. 10. It was tiring because of the early start, the sickness and the long walk, but it was happy because of the beautiful sunrise and the kind tea-shop owner.

Reading 4

A. 1. (b) 2. (a) 3. (b) 4. (c) 5. (a). B. 6. Mobile phones, radio and television. 7. A good teacher in the capital can reach the classroom through a recorded or live lesson. 8. They cannot ask questions as easily as in a classroom. 9.

Many homes have no smartphone and the signal is weak. 10. A mixture of ordinary classes and online material. C. 11. (b). 12. (c). 13. (e). 14. (a). 15. (d).

Guided writing I: model

How to make a paper boat You need: one rectangular sheet of paper.

  1. Fold the sheet in half along its length, then open it to leave a centre line.
  2. Fold the top corners down to the centre line to make a triangle at the top.
  3. Fold the lower strips up on both sides over the triangle.
  4. Open the folded paper and flatten it into a diamond.
  5. Fold the lower corners up and open again to form a boat.
  6. Pull the two tips gently apart and set the boat on water.
Guided writing II: model

The shepherd boy and the wolf

A shepherd boy looked after sheep near a village. One day he was bored, so he cried, "Wolf! Wolf!" The villagers ran to help, but found no wolf, and the boy laughed. He played the same trick again. One evening a real wolf came.

The boy cried for help, but no one believed him, and the wolf scattered the flock. Moral: a liar is not believed even when he tells the truth.

Free writing I: model

Customer: Good morning. I bought this phone from you last week, but the screen flickers. Shopkeeper: I am sorry to hear that. May I see the bill? Customer: Here it is. I have also brought the box and the charger. Shopkeeper: Thank you.

Has the phone been dropped? Customer: No, it has not. The fault started on the second day. Shopkeeper: In that case it is covered by the warranty. I can replace it today or send it for repair.

Customer: I would like a replacement, please. Shopkeeper: Certainly. Please wait for a few minutes while I get a new one. Customer: Thank you for your help.

Free writing II: model

Kathmandu 20 Poush 2082

Dear Sapana,

I hope you are well. I am writing to tell you about the trip I took with my class last week. We went to Chitwan for three days. We left at six in the morning and reached by noon after a long, noisy bus ride. In the afternoon we visited the elephant breeding centre.

The next morning we went on a jeep safari. We saw deer, a rhinoceros and many birds. In the evening we watched a Tharu stick dance and tried to join in. Our teacher joked that I would never be a dancer!

On the last day we took a canoe ride on the river. Everyone was tired but happy. I wish you had come. Please write to me soon and tell me about your holiday.

Yours lovingly, Pratima

Grammar

A. 1. will have finished (finished before a point in the future). 2. aren't I. 3. The officer asked me where I lived. 4. My bicycle has been stolen. 5. How does she go to school? B. 6. (b) is — the number of is singular. 7.

(b) stay — a number of is plural. 8. (b) got — get + person + to + verb; had, let and made take the bare infinitive. 9. (b) Although. 10. (a) rains — present tense after if in a first conditional.

10.4 Predicted questions

How this list is ranked

The priority order below reflects how often each task type is asked (every paper includes four reading passages, four writing tasks and ten grammar items) and how much weight each text or task carries.

Tier A: practise before anything else

Rank Question Reason
1 A formal or personal letter (Free writing II) The largest writing slot (9 marks); a letter is the commonest form
2 An essay on a social or educational topic The other half of the same slot
3 An application (leave or job) Free writing I names both
4 A notice, an advertisement or a chart description Guided writing I names them
5 A news story or a story from a skeleton Guided writing II names them
6 Reading 4 on an essay or article, with a vocabulary item 15 marks, the largest single reading task
7 Grammar: reported speech, passive, tense, tag, conditional Five reproduction items
8 The seen texts of Units 8 to 11 Short texts; true/false and matching items are easy to set

Tier B: likely second line

Rank Question Reason
9 "Climbing", "Weathers", "If" The poems are short and fit the 100-word seen slot
10 "Pratap Malla" and "Flowers in Russian Culture" Facts and dates make good MCQs and gap-fills
11 "Expect the Unexpected" and "Sugarloaf Mountain" Place descriptions give facts for matching
12 "Hachi: A Dog's Tale" and "Interesting Social Media Stories" Review and article give MCQs
13 An email or a dialogue Free writing I and II name them
14 A biography or a condolence message Guided writing II names them
15 Grammar MCQs: articles, prepositions, connectives, agreement Five MCQ items

Tier C: smaller but still in the syllabus

Rank Question Reason
16 "Cabbage White" and "Parents" Stories; short-answer on plot or irony
17 "Population" and "bird migration" Figures give gap-fill items
18 "Wisdom of Little Girls" and "World Record" Moral and satire
19 Instructions or a recipe Guided writing I names them
20 Causatives and relative clauses Smaller grammar topics
Using this list in the last two weeks

Week 1: write one letter, one application, one essay, one notice and one news story and mark each against the models. Week 2: re-read two seen texts a day, write five true/false items for each, then do a full model set in three hours.

Chapter summary

  • The paper is Reading 40 (5 + 10 + 10 + 15), Writing 25 (5 + 5 + 6 + 9) and Grammar 10 = 75 marks in 3 hours.
  • Seen-text items are answered from the book; unseen items from the passage in front of you.
  • Writing is marked on format and organisation first: a letter needs an address, date, subject line and closing; a news story needs a headline and a dateline.
  • Grammar: nobody gets a positive tag, aren't I, the number of is singular, a number of is plural, if + present → will.
  • The ranking above comes from the grid and the syllabus, not from any knowledge of the paper.

Practice questions

Short questions (1 mark each)

  1. Who wrote "Weathers"? [1]
  2. In which year was the modern Olympic Games first held? [1]
  3. Add a question tag: Nobody came, ____? [1]
  4. Change into the passive: They are building a road. [1]
Answers to Short questions

1. Thomas Hardy.

2. 1896, in Athens.

3. did they.

4. A road is being built.

Writing (5 to 9 marks)

  1. Write a news story from these clues: Bus accident — Mugling — Monday morning — 12 injured — hospital. [5]
  2. Write an essay of about 200 words on The Role of Teachers in Society. [9]
Answers to Writing

1. Use the news-story model in Chapter 9, section 9.4: headline, dateline, who, what, when, where, why and one closing line.

2. Use the essay model in section 9.6 of the previous chapter: introduction, three body points with examples, a conclusion.
